newsitem.title: KENYA: Restrictions said undermining Kenya bourse growth.
newsitem.headline: Restrictions said undermining Kenya bourse growth.

text.p: Restrictive foreign investment rules and ignorance on stock investment possibilities in Kenya have undermined a faster growth of the Nairobi Stock Exchange (NSE), bourse officials and brokers said on Thursday.
They said that some 17 blue chip companies from the 58 listed on the Nairobi bourse were majority foreign-owned and under Kenyan laws were not open to foreign portfolio investors.
They said foreign portfolio investors were left with the option of putting their money into shares that were essentially not very attractive and were literally forced to stay away.
The bourse officials and brokers spoke in an interview with "Africa Journal", a Reuters Television programme.
A senior bourse official said a majority of the Kenyan population was also still ignorant about investment in equities, although the bourse had begun a programme to improve awareness.
In majority Kenyan-owned companies, foreign portfolio investment may run up to 40 percent and no single investor can hold more than a 5.0 percent stake in one company.

"Because of the 40 percent investment gap for international investors, they have not been so keen to invest and instead have turned to offshore investments," said John Munge, managing director of leading brokerage house Shah, Munge & Partners Ltd.

"It is important to note that the government currently allows foreigners to invest in locally controlled companies and yet 17 blue chip companies are foreign controlled; that means foreign portfolio investors cannot access them," Munge added.
Munge said high interest rates on government treasury bills -- in the range of 18-25 percent -- and a slow clearance method were the other obstacles against a faster bourse growth.
Clearance at the bourse is seven days after a deal. A central depository system to be launched sometime next year will end the delay and ensure faster slow of money, brokers said.

Robert Mathu, manager for trading and operations at the Nairobi Stock Exchange, said: "The biggest obstacle (among Kenyans) has been understanding the concept of the stock market which is now becoming clearer."
He said the population was "fairly aware" and pointed to increasing amounts of cash invested in shares.
"However, the market is still slow and, because of that, most shareholders will not be encouraged to sell shares especially if they want to make good profit," Mathu added.

Mathu said government privatisation of companies through the stock exchange had so far been successful. This year such success has been seen in Kenya Airways, National Bank of Kenya and Kenya Commercial Bank.

"Companies should opt for capitalization through the bourse since it is a less costly method of raising funds, opens up activity to the public and a share price is a yardstick for performance of the company in the market," Mathu said.
Kenyan family-based concerns have been reluctant to list for fear of losing control, according to market experts in Nairobi.
The Nairobi bourse, with a capitalisation of $1.8 billion, is the fourth largest in Africa behind the stock exchanges in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Egypt.
